c.tagline: Sunlit coast, paella, and futuristic architecture.

emergency.note: 091 national police, 092 local police and 061 health emergencies also work; 112 operators usually offer English.

hood_landmark.Ciutat Vella: Valencia Cathedral with its climbable Miguelete bell tower
hood_landmark.Ruzafa (Russafa): Mercado de Ruzafa, the colorful modernist market hall
hood_landmark.El Carmen: Torres de Serranos, the medieval city gate
hood_landmark.El Cabanyal: colorful tiled fishermen's houses steps from Malvarrosa beach
hood_landmark.Eixample: Mercado de Colón, the ornate modernista market

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing on Malvarrosa beach, in the centre and around the stations

hood_desc: Ciutat Vella is the historic old town and tourist heart, home to the cathedral, Plaza de la Reina and the Central Market, ideal for first-time visitors who want landmarks and museums within walking distance.
Ruzafa (Russafa) is the trendy, bohemian district packed with cafes, vintage shops, tapas bars and nightlife, perfect for younger travelers, foodies and creatives who want a hip local scene.
El Carmen is the oldest medieval quarter with narrow winding streets, street art and lively bars, best suited to nightlife lovers and those seeking an artsy, atmospheric stay.
El Cabanyal is the colorful former fishermen quarter beside the beach, increasingly hip with great seafood and tiled houses, great for beach lovers wanting an authentic, less touristy neighborhood.
Eixample is an elegant, upscale grid district with modernist architecture, refined restaurants and a calm residential feel, suited to travelers who want a quieter, sophisticated base near the center.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.pay: Rides use the rechargeable SUMA10 smartcard, sold and topped up at metro/tram machines and EMT points; contactless bank cards are not yet accepted at the gates, only Metrovalencia's own smartcards. A single ticket costs from €1.50 for one zone up to €4.80 for the widest zone (about $1.65-5.30), and a 1-day SUMA T pass starts at €4 (about $4.40).
transit.hours: Metro and trams run from around 5:30am until about midnight (some lines finish nearer 11pm); EMT buses run through the evening, with a handful of Nitbus night lines on Friday and Saturday nights.

transit.m: Metro line 3/5 to Xativa or Colon, 25 min
Bus line 150 to city center, 40-45 min

food.name: Paella valenciana
food.desc: Rabbit, chicken, flat green beans and garrofo beans over bomba rice cooked on orange wood - no chorizo, and always at lunch.

places.name: Casa Carmela
places.note: Cooked over wood fires since 1922 by the beach; book days in advance.

places.name: La Pepica
places.note: Open since 1898 on the seafront promenade; the historic paella house.

places.name: Navarro
places.note: Central 1960s arroceria doing a dozen rice dishes for city-centre lunches.

food.name: All i pebre
food.desc: Albufera eel stewed with potatoes, garlic and sweet paprika until the broth thickens; the lagoon villages' signature pot.

places.name: Nou Raco
places.note: Lagoon-side dining room with boat trips; all i pebre plus arroces.

places.name: Restaurante Bon Aire
places.note: Family house in the eel-fishing village; go for lunch after the lagoon.

places.name: Casa Carmina
places.note: Long-running rice and eel kitchen between the city and the Albufera.

food.name: Esmorzaret
food.desc: The mid-morning Valencian ritual: a huge filled bread roll, peanuts, olives, a cremaet coffee and a small beer, around 10am.

places.name: Bar Ricardo
places.note: Old-school bar famous for its almuerzo bocadillos and fried seafood.

places.name: Casa Guillermo
places.note: Anchovy specialist since 1952; stand at the bar with a vermut.

places.name: Central Bar
places.note: Ricard Camarena's counter inside the market; sandwiches from market produce.

food.name: Fideua and arros a banda
food.desc: Short noodles or plain rice cooked in fish stock and eaten with garlic allioli - the seafarers' answer to paella.

places.name: Casa Montana
places.note: Barrel-lined bodega from 1836 in the fishermen's quarter; superb tapas too.

places.name: La Pepica
places.note: Seafront classic where fideua sits beside the paella on the menu.

places.name: Casa Carmela
places.note: Wood-fired rices including arros a banda; reserve well ahead.

food.name: Bunuelos de calabaza
food.desc: Airy pumpkin fritters fried to order and dunked in thick chocolate; everywhere during Fallas, findable year-round.

places.name: Horchateria Santa Catalina
places.note: Tiled 19th-century salon serving chocolate and fritters all day.

places.name: Mercat Central
places.note: Market stalls frying bunuelos and churros beside the produce counters.

food.name: Horchata con fartons
food.desc: Iced tiger-nut milk from nearby Alboraya with long soft sugar-glazed buns made purely for dipping; an afternoon institution.

places.name: Horchateria Santa Catalina
places.note: The city's most famous horchateria, open daily beside Santa Catalina church.

places.name: Horchateria Daniel
places.note: Alboraya house with a counter in the modernist market hall.

places.name: Horchateria El Siglo
places.note: Quieter old-town alternative a short walk from the cathedral.

food.name: Agua de Valencia
food.desc: Cava, fresh orange juice, gin and vodka served by the jug - deceptively easy, invented in the city in the 1950s.

places.name: Cafe de las Horas
places.note: Baroque, candlelit bar most associated with the drink; jugs to share.

places.name: Cafe Sant Jaume
places.note: Former pharmacy turned bar on the old town's busiest street.

food.name: Vermut de grifo and Utiel-Requena wine
food.desc: House vermouth poured from the tap before lunch, and juicy Bobal reds from the Utiel-Requena hills inland.

places.name: Casa Montana
places.note: Hundreds of Spanish references and vermouth straight from the barrel.

places.name: Mercado de Colon
places.note: Modernist hall with vermouth and wine counters busy at weekend aperitif hour.

landmarks: City of Arts and Sciences
A futuristic complex of white, sculptural buildings by Santiago Calatrava that is Valencia's most photographed modern icon.
L'Oceanografic
Europe's largest aquarium, part of the Arts and Sciences complex, offers striking modern architecture above and below water.
Valencia Cathedral
A Gothic-Romanesque-Baroque cathedral said to house the Holy Grail, with the climbable Miguelete bell tower offering city views.
La Lonja de la Seda (Silk Exchange)
A UNESCO World Heritage Gothic silk exchange famed for its twisting stone columns and ornate hall.
Mercado Central (Central Market)
One of Europe's oldest working markets, its Art Nouveau ironwork and stained glass make for a colorful, bustling photo subject.
Torres de Serranos
A monumental 14th-century medieval city gate that once guarded Valencia and remains a striking silhouette against the sky.
Torres de Quart
Sturdy 15th-century fortified gate towers still scarred by cannonball marks from the Napoleonic siege.
Plaza de Toros de Valencia
A grand neoclassical bullring modeled on Roman amphitheaters, an emblematic circular landmark near the train station.
Palau de la Música de Valencia
A glass-domed concert hall whose transparent, crystalline design makes it a standout piece of modern architecture.
Jardín del Turia (Turia Gardens)
A lush 9km park built in the former riverbed, offering green, sweeping vistas that connect many of the city's landmarks.

train.note: No international trains run from Valencia. AVE high-speed trains from Valencia Joaquín Sorolla reach Madrid in about 2h and Barcelona (via a change or direct AVE) in around 3h, with connections onward across Spain. For France, take a coach or connect through Barcelona.

bus.note: Long-distance and international coaches use the Estació d'Autobusos de València on the north side of the city. FlixBus, ALSA and BlaBlaCar Bus run overnight services toward France - carry ID for the border.

ferry.note: Ferries leave from the Port of València. Baleària sails to Algeria (Mostaganem and Algiers) - bring your passport and check visa rules. Its frequent boats to the Balearic Islands (Palma, Ibiza, Mahón), also run by Trasmed and GNV, are domestic Spanish routes.

half.name: Albufera Natural Park
half.blurb: Tranquil freshwater lagoon ringed by rice paddies, birdlife and sunset boat rides near the coast.

half.name: Sagunto
half.blurb: Hilltop town crowned by a sprawling castle and a well-preserved Roman theatre overlooking the sea.

half.name: Xàtiva
half.blurb: Historic town beneath a long ridge-top castle, birthplace of two Borgia popes.

half.name: Peñíscola
half.blurb: Walled seaside old town on a rocky promontory, famous for its Templar castle and beaches.

half.name: Requena
half.blurb: Historic wine town in the Utiel-Requena region known for cellars, bodegas and cured meats.

half.name: Albarracín
half.blurb: Enchanting medieval hill town of pink-hued houses and walls above a river gorge.
